extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, journalists, and researchers interested in journalism ethics and scandals
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and describe the ethical standards, common failures, and newsroom practices that define or prevent journalistic scandals. Useful for analyzing incidents where journalism's accepted norms were breached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic standard referencing honesty as a core expectation of journalists and news organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honesty is cited as a typical standard that journalists are expected to follow; breaches of honesty are a primary driver of scandals because they call into question integrity and truthfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding journalistic bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The expectation that journalists avoid introducing bias into reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoiding bias is listed among customary expectations/standards; failures in this area can lead to public perceptions that reporting is unfair or slanted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should demonstrate responsibility in their reporting and conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsibility is enumerated as a typical standard; lack of responsibility (e.g., sloppy verification) contributes to scandals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between privacy and public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Striking an appropriate balance between individuals' privacy and the public's right to know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This balance is called out as a typical standard; misjudging it can produce ethical breaches or scandals (e.g., unnecessary invasion of privacy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shunning financial or romantic conflict of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoiding financial or romantic conflicts of interest that could affect coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explicitly lists shunning financial or romantic conflict of interest; later examples note newsroom rules requiring staff to disclose relationships and sometimes recuse or be reassigned to avoid appearance of conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing ethical means to obtain information
rubrics_metrics.description: Using ethical (non-deceptive, lawful) methods to gather reporting materials and sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page groups 'choosing ethical means to obtain information' among typical standards; unethical sourcing methods (e.g., deceptive practices) are implicated in scandals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Copying others' work or ideas without attribution, identified as a common element of journalistic scandals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plagiarism is listed alongside fabrication and omission as a central type of scandalous conduct that undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventing facts, quotes, sources, or events; explicitly cited as a core cause of journalism scandals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabrication (making up material) is singled out as a scandal characteristic; high-profile examples on the page (e.g., Stephen Glass, Claas Relotius) illustrate consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of information
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to include relevant facts or context in reporting, which can constitute a scandal when deliberate or reckless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omission is grouped with plagiarism and fabrication as a common characteristic of scandals; omission can mislead audiences even without outright fabrication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activities that violate the law or ethical rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in illegal acts or breaches of ethical rules during reporting or newsgathering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes that scandals can include activities that violate the law or ethical rules, implying that legality and adherence to codes are evaluative standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Altering or staging events being documented
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulating, staging, or altering events or evidence that are purportedly being reported as real.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Altering or staging an event being documented is called out as a scandalous practice because it directly falsifies what journalism claims to represent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial reporting or researching errors leading to libel/defamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale errors in reporting or research that result in libelous or defamatory statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explicitly mentions substantial errors that lead to libel or defamation as a type of scandal, highlighting the legal and reputational risks of poor verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintaining credibility and truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserving journalism's integrity, truthfulness, and public trust; credibility described as journalism's main currency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because all scandals 'call into question the integrity and truthfulness of journalism,' maintaining credibility is emphasized as a foundational criterion; loss of credibility shifts scrutiny to the media itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict codes of conduct and enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Having and enforcing written codes of conduct and newsroom policies to prevent ethical breaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes many outlets maintain strict codes of conduct and enforce them; such codes and enforcement are preventative measures and serve as criteria against which behavior is judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial oversight and multiple layers of checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of layered editorial oversight (editors, fact-checkers, etc.) to catch problems before publication or broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several layers of editorial oversight are described as mechanisms to catch problems; the page also documents cases where these checks failed, indicating the importance of robust oversight and its role in evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure, recusal, and reassignment policies for conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies requiring staff to disclose relationships or conflicts, recuse themselves from certain coverage, or be reassigned to avoid appearance of conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page quotes guidance (example from a newspaper) that staff who develop close relationships with people who might figure in coverage must disclose them and may need to recuse or be reassigned; these procedural rules are part of assessing ethical compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding rushed publication at the expense of checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Resisting the rush to publish 'breaking' news if it causes omission of verification and editorial checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes scandals can occur when checks and balances are omitted in the rush to get an important story to press or on air, identifying speed-vs-accuracy trade-offs as an evaluative concern.
